The Preposterous Awesomeness of Everything, developed by Joe Richardson and published by Akupara Games, is a quirky and satirical point-and-click adventure that defies traditional game conventions through its absurd humor, unique art style, and social commentary. Released in early 2016, the game immediately grabs attention with its offbeat premise: a primitive society ambitiously attempts to build a space rocket using only glue and tape. This outlandish setup serves as a backdrop for a larger exploration of themes like progress, politics, and human nature, all presented through a lens of irreverent comedy and sharp wit.

Players guide a chaotic group known simply as the Majority of People as they transition from a state of disorder into a rough approximation of democracy, all while striving for the impossible goal of reaching outer space. Along the way, the story introduces a cast of peculiar and memorable characters, including the enigmatic Man with the Little Pencil, the oddly dressed Man in the Wren Suit, and the flamboyant Helen. These figures are more than just quirky personalities—they act as vehicles for the game’s satirical take on societal structures, bureaucracy, and the often absurd behaviors that define human civilization. The dialogue is peppered with humor that is sometimes subtle and other times overtly ridiculous, encouraging players to reflect on the underlying commentary even as they laugh at the bizarre situations.

One of the most striking aspects of The Preposterous Awesomeness of Everything is its distinct visual presentation. Rather than adopting typical pixel art or realistic graphics, the game employs a collage-based aesthetic that feels raw and decidedly human. This patchwork style, composed of cut-out images and mismatched elements, reinforces the game's themes of improvisation and disorder. It feels intentionally unfinished, mirroring the chaotic and makeshift world the Majority of People inhabit. The interface itself refreshes the classic verb-based point-and-click style by adding playful and unconventional verbs such as “befuddle,” “disrespect,” and “pray-for,” which expand the ways players can interact with their environment and deepen the sense of quirky immersion.

While the game’s humor and artistic vision are widely appreciated, it is not without its criticisms. Some players and reviewers have found the narrative to be somewhat lacking in depth and cohesion, with moments where the satire feels surface-level rather than deeply insightful. The gameplay, while creatively designed, can at times feel disjointed or less engaging compared to more traditional adventure games. This unevenness in pacing and storytelling has led to mixed reactions—some praise the game for its boldness and originality, while others feel it falls short of delivering a fully satisfying experience. Additionally, the abstract nature of the humor and the unusual art style might not resonate with everyone, making it a niche title that appeals mostly to those who appreciate unconventional storytelling and experimental design.

Despite these drawbacks, The Preposterous Awesomeness of Everything offers a fresh and thought-provoking experience that stands out in the crowded adventure game genre. Its blend of absurd comedy and social critique invites players to look beyond surface-level entertainment and engage with the themes of progress, governance, and human folly in a playful yet meaningful way. For fans of Joe Richardson’s work or those seeking a game that challenges traditional narrative forms, this title provides a compelling, if unconventional, journey. Ultimately, it is a game that rewards patience and curiosity, inviting players to embrace its chaotic charm and appreciate the preposterous awesomeness woven into every aspect of its design.

I never played a Joe Richardson game before. Since his last game Death of the Reprobate came out last year (November '24), the adventure game community already started laughing with the anticipation of laughing with everything the game would have to offer. Instead of playing it immediately like everyone else seemed to have done, I decided to travel back in time (not literally) and play through ALL of Joe Richardson's games available on Steam, starting with The Preposterous Awesomeness of Everything.

After playing for 9 minutes, I got tired of it. I knew the graphic style and character designs would need some getting used to. And yes, that was the case. Also, stupid me got "stuck" by not realizing the screen could sidescroll. So after I don't know how much time and other games went by, I decided to return and lo and behold, the game actually grew on me. I started to appreciate the social, political, anthropological, philosophical satire -- and of course the plain silliness of it all. Though is it really silly? I think a part of me really thinks it's brilliant.

So you play a guy on an island, you find old rocket parts and you decide to engage everyone to build it up again. A couple of other islanders grab leadership, however, but don't really succeed in getting anywhere with society since they take turns in being elected and spend all their time nullifying all progress of their predecessor; basically the way actual politicians conduct their business today.

The game is very short, I finished it in 97 minutes. It has some inventory puzzles, some dialogue puzzles, some main character trickery onto non-playable characters. It doesn't have a manual save function but autosaves whenever you make some progress. Its cutscenes are storybook-style text and pictures that are quite fun to read. Joe Richardson truly is a funny guy who gets his message across.

So in the end, not a bad game at all, and I'm looking forward to the next one, Four Last Things...

Definitely worth a play if you're a fan of Joe Richardson's later works, where he really cracked the art that worked best with his animation style, and told the story more subtly.

[b] The Preposterous Awesomeness of Everything [/b] is one of the best pieces of satire in gaming I have played in a long time, possibly ever, I don't know.

It's topical, it's relevant, it's probably timeless which is depressing. It makes no sense. And it is SO. FUNNY.

Its bitter self-indulgent scathing mockery of the human race and our social-political hierarchies is SO on point it almost makes the base of my skull hurt. 

It's bureaucracy growing from diapers into adulthood. It's a cage match between nihilism and absurdism.  It's feeling isolated by your own frustration at how your fellow humans blissfully c*ck everything up (and maybe a little bit of shame when you see yourself in that soup mix too, if we're being honest). 

You can't help but shake your head laughing in the kind of way that you just understand something to be a fundamental truth even though it's moronic and ridiculous. 

It narrowly escapes coming off as arrogant. 

I don't even care if it was amateur and sometimes lazy game design.

It's ugly as sin but doesn't matter because it's just the vehicle for the hearty dialogue. After a while it feels... charming? 

It's a short play but the premise is dense so I didn't mind at all. And as always with me there were a couple things I had to look up because I just wasn't following the logic but then those things made perfect sense. 

I played this [i] after [/i] I played the [b] Immortal John Triptych [/b] and not that my opinion really matters at all whatsoever but I wish Joe would've baked this format of [b] TPAoE [/b] longer. I think it was much more original in concept and execution as well as authentic in messaging. 

Might not be for everyone but I believe in you, Joe, even though you crapped the bed with [b] Death of the Reprobate. [/b] 5/5

TPAoE is an experimental point & click made by one man who describes himself as an inexperienced "twit with a dream." It doesn't try to have high production value; it prefers to focus its effort in being different. There's no voice acting, barely any music, and it's only 2 hours long. But what it gets right kept me engaged for its entire runtime, even if I can't say I left the experience with some profound takeaway (though it definitely tried).

The writing is good (even if it's in wall-of-text form sometimes), and I enjoyed its satire. I thought the art fit the theme (and budget) quite well, and was one of the strongest aspects of the entire package. The puzzles were dead simple, which is my preference in adventure games (getting stuck for hours clicking around is my personal hell), so i can't complain there.

The satire is the core of what this game should be evaluated on, and though I think it's well written and funny, it's rather ... simple. Themes it satirizes include: "Both political parties are two sides of the same coin; interested solely in maintaining their power", "Politicians lie", "The majority of people are sheep who are too numb and dumb to think anything but what they're told to think by the media", etc. These are topics not commonly covered in games, so I greatly appreciate that they're here, but they're also rather surface level. None of it is particularly poorly done, but none of it is exceptionally well done either.

I had fun with the game though, and I always have to hand it to an artist who's baring their soul. I'll play Joe's other games (already bought them!); curious to see what they're like after this.

This game is either an ugly, basic point and click adventure with puzzles so simple that i spent the most time trying to work out how to get the 'Death by jumping' achievement... Or it's a clever, critical condemnation of modern society, including politics, and the cruel futility of life.
What starts as a slightly odd adventure game, quickly reveals itself as a witty, if a little on-the-nose critique of 'happiness' in the modern world, and the pointlessness of both conformity, and even counter-cultures.

Either way, the art-style is ugly (rather impressively, it's uglier in motion that the screenshots suggest), but has cute overtones of Python, Spitting Image (and perhaps South Park).  The sound design is minimal (except for a few musical motifs in some areas it's mostly missing) and there's no speech (tragic, but i doubt the author's budget would have extended to voice actors that would do the game's intent justice). Despite these failings, it's surprisingly pleasing to play, and rarely does it feel like a particular area has out-stayed its welcome.

Overall, I can't help but feel that this game deserves to be played and recommended by more people.   I played through it about 2.5x in the 100 minutes i spent with it (mostly to wrap the achievements, though there is some light 'replay' appeal that i don't want to spoil), and at the sale price ($3 CAD) I consider that a price worth paying.  I look forward to playing the other two games (which are actually the reason I picked this up).
